title: Sanity Deep Dive
body:
# Sanity Deep Dive — Why a role or token change "didn't work"

*After this, you can explain why a permission change can look like it did nothing, and walk a customer through confirming what's actually granted right now.*

::: {.callout}
**The short version:** A role change propagates to the Content Lake within seconds, but a Studio tab that's already open has its own cached copy of the old permissions — reloading, not waiting, is the fix. A robot token is worse: its permissions can't be edited in place at all, only replaced. And permissions are additive across every role a member holds, so a new, more restrictive role never revokes access a broader role already grants.
:::

## Why this comes up

Two ticket shapes, same root cause: "I changed Sarah's role from Viewer to Editor but she still can't publish," or "I locked down my robot token's permissions and it's still doing the thing I tried to stop." In both cases the customer assumes the change silently failed, when it actually applied — the customer just isn't looking at the place where it applied.

## How it actually works

**Role changes apply server-side almost immediately.** Per Sanity's docs, "when you create or modify a role via the Access API, Sanity propagates the change to the Content Lake, typically within seconds. After propagation, the new permissions apply to the user's or robot's next request." That's the server side settled.

**A running Studio session doesn't know that yet.** The same docs call this out directly: "a running Studio app may show stale permission state until the user reloads." Studio reads permissions once per session and holds onto them client-side, so a user who was already in Studio when their role changed is working from a stale picture until they refresh the tab (or sign out and back in).

**A robot token's permissions can't be changed in place.** The Access API's `PUT` endpoint for an existing robot "accepts `expiresAt` and no other fields: to change a token's label or memberships, create a new token and delete the old one." So "I edited the token's permissions" isn't a supported action — whatever roles the token was created with are the roles it has, until it's replaced.

**Permissions only add up, never subtract.** This is the one that surprises people designing custom roles: "permissions are additive in nature. That means you cannot remove a permission that has been granted elsewhere, either by another content resource on the same role or by another role that the same member holds." A member holding a narrow custom role *and* the stock Editor role still gets full Editor access — the narrow role doesn't constrain anything, it only adds.

## Walk it through

To find out what a user or token can actually do right now, rather than guessing from the roles screen, call the Access API's own check endpoint with that user's or token's session:

```bash
curl -s \
  "https://api.sanity.io/v2025-07-11/access/project/<projectId>/user-permissions/me/check?permissions=sanity.project.members.read" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <theirToken>"
```

This asks the API what the caller can do at this instant, server-side — no Studio cache in the way. If it confirms the permission is granted but the user still can't do the thing in Studio, the problem is client-side staleness, not a propagation failure: have them reload.

Contrast that with trying to "fix" a robot token by changing its permissions:

```bash
# This does NOT work — PUT only accepts expiresAt
curl -X PUT "https://api.sanity.io/v2026-07-10/access/project/<projectId>/robots/<robotId>" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SANITY_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"roleNames": ["viewer"]}'
# → rejected / silently ignored beyond expiresAt

# This is the supported path: create the replacement, then delete the old one
curl -X POST "https://api.sanity.io/v2026-07-10/access/project/<projectId>/robots" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SANITY_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"label":"build-pipeline-v2","memberships":[{"resourceType":"project","resourceId":"<projectId>","roleNames":["viewer"]}]}'

curl -X DELETE "https://api.sanity.io/v2026-07-10/access/project/<projectId>/robots/<oldRobotId>" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SANITY_TOKEN"
```

## Where it goes wrong

|Symptom|Cause|Fix|
|  ---  |  ---  |  ---  |
|"I changed their role but Studio still shows the old options"|Studio caches permissions for the session|Reload the browser tab (or fully sign out/in)|
|"The new role doesn't seem to apply to API calls yet"|Rare propagation lag (normally seconds)|Wait briefly, then confirm with the `user-permissions/me/check` endpoint before assuming it's broken|
|"I updated my robot token's permissions and nothing changed"|The robot `PUT` endpoint only accepts `expiresAt` — memberships/roles can't be mutated in place|Create a new token with the right roles, cut over, then delete the old one|
|"I gave them a restrictive custom role but they can still do everything"|Permissions are additive — a broader role held elsewhere (e.g. stock Editor) still applies|Audit every role the member holds, not just the one just edited|
|"The dataset role says No access but people still read published content"|The dataset is public — public datasets grant published-content read regardless of role|Expected behavior; if this must be locked down, change dataset visibility, not the role|

## Triage checklist

1. Confirm the surface: is the "no effect" happening in the Studio UI, or in raw API/token behavior? The fix differs.
2. If it's Studio: have the user hard-reload the tab. This is a client-side cache, not a server propagation issue, so waiting longer won't help.
3. If it's an API or token question: call `GET /v2025-07-11/access/{resourceType}/{resourceId}/user-permissions/me/check` with that identity's credentials to see the server's current answer, independent of any UI.
4. If the check confirms the grant is correct but behavior still looks wrong: look for another role the same user or token holds. Permissions are additive — a broader grant elsewhere is very often the real explanation.
5. If this is a robot token and the customer says they "edited its permissions": ask whether they used the token's three-dot menu (expiry only) or tried a direct API update. Either way, changing a token's roles requires creating a new one and deleting the old one.
6. If the concern is read access on a public dataset: this isn't a role bug. Public datasets always allow read of published content; the role setting only ever restricts private datasets or unpublished content.

::: {.callout}
**Say this to the customer:** Role and token changes apply on our servers almost immediately, but a couple of things can make it look otherwise. If you changed someone's role while they had Studio open, ask them to refresh their browser tab — Studio holds onto permissions for the length of a session. If you're trying to change what an existing API token is allowed to do, that's not something we support in place: tokens keep the permissions they were created with, so the way to change them is to create a new token with the access you want and remove the old one. And if someone holds more than one role, keep in mind permissions only add up — they never take access away that another role already granted.
:::

## Going deeper

* [Roles and permissions](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/roles-concepts) — concepts, default roles, how custom-role changes propagate, and the verification endpoint.
* [Roles (user guide)](https://www.sanity.io/docs/user-guides/roles) — assigning roles, the additive-permissions gotcha, and the public-dataset read gotcha.
* [Authentication and tokens](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/http-auth) — personal vs. robot tokens, token expiry, and why the robot `PUT` endpoint only accepts `expiresAt`.
* [Build a custom role with the Access API](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/build-a-custom-role-with-the-access-api) — recipes for scoped and attribute-based custom roles.
* Related changelog: [Manage — Review your security posture in one place](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/334072af-b48d-4e08-a5e2-2dfe3e177a8c) (Sep 1, 2026) and [Manage — Prevent non-SAML users from joining your organization](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/9acad526-2b71-46f7-b274-bd21a0a4d64a) (Sep 25, 2026), both touching how role and access assignment show up in Manage.

title: Morning Debrief
body:
# Morning Debrief — September 29, 2026

*What's new at Sanity, for support. Items marked :new: shipped in the last 24 hours; the rest are the most recent relevant changes.*

## :rocket: Releases

* :new: **Sanity Context v2.1.0** (Sep 28, 2026) — `@sanity/context` now supports both AI SDK v6 and v7, fixing the `Export bindTelemetryIntegration doesn't exist in target module` build error people hit when upgrading to `ai@7`; on v7 telemetry moves to `telemetry: {integrations: [...]}` and `isEnabled` is dropped, while existing v6 setups using `experimental_telemetry` keep working unchanged. → [Changelog entry](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/context-pkg-Mi4xLjA)
    * *Why it matters: this is the first ticket-shaped question you'll get from anyone bumping the AI SDK — the fix is a version bump, not a config rewrite.*
* **MCP server v2.36.0** (Sep 25, 2026) — tools that take a workspace name now default to the only available workspace when none is passed, plus compatibility fixes for asset upload responses and free-form document/asset inputs. → [Changelog entry](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/9b5d7467-d051-47d7-9fa8-5df70baad579)
* **MCP server v2.35.4** (Sep 24, 2026) — MCP deployments now bundle Sanity Studio 6.14.1, so agent-deployed Studios pick up the Portable Text data fix without any action from the customer. → [Changelog entry](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/8eaebac3-a74c-4a0c-980c-2027106b8fcd)

## :sparkles: New features

* :new: **Expanded documentation for Sanity Context, Functions, and Presentation** (Sanity Docs, Sep 29, 2026) — two months of docs work landed at once: a restructured Sanity Context section organized by task, four new Knowledge Base guides (creating one, source types, keeping it current, resolving issues), framework guides for the Vercel AI SDK, LangChain, and the OpenAI Agents SDK, upgrade guides for every Studio major version, and new troubleshooting docs for Agent Actions, dataset backups, and account management. → [Changelog entry](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/d8bf2c5c-3030-49c8-8e47-e487f59048b1)
    * *Why it matters: there is now a documented migration path off the Context Studio plugin to the Context app, plus a "Content access and security" page explaining how the organization token, MCP sources, and `groqFilter` together decide what a connected agent can read — link it instead of explaining it from scratch.*
* **Prevent non-SAML users from joining an organization** (Manage, Sep 25, 2026) — Enterprise org admins can flip a setting in SAML SSO settings so only a SAML identity from the org can accept an invitation or request access; it is off by default and does not remove existing non-SAML members, who must be removed separately. Worth warning customers that Sanity does not merge duplicate accounts, so roles should be verified on each SAML identity first. → [Changelog entry](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/9acad526-2b71-46f7-b274-bd21a0a4d64a)
* **Folder descriptions in Media Library** (Media Library, Sep 23, 2026) — descriptions can be added when creating a folder or edited later in the sidebar. → [Changelog entry](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/fdfa3ee8-4c00-4350-8c88-5728a1f873ce)

## :bug: Bug fixes

* **Tool inputs rejected or silently ignored by the MCP server** (MCP server v2.35.3, Sep 23, 2026) — JSON-stringified legacy resource objects are now accepted, `create_documents` accepts JSON-stringified document arrays and content objects, and misplaced top-level fields are rejected outright instead of being silently dropped. If a customer reported documents created with missing fields via an agent, this is the likely cause. → [Changelog entry](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/9acdf0f9-f07b-4ac7-a5ad-98c6b30106a7)
* **Media Library filter menus, deletion safeguards, and reconnection** (Media Library, Sep 23, 2026) — filter menus now render and scroll correctly on short screens, asset deletion is disabled when the usage check fails (with a tooltip saying why), and the Library reconnects and refreshes cached content after a network interruption or expired auth. → [Changelog entry](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/fdfa3ee8-4c00-4350-8c88-5728a1f873ce)
* **Editor crash on unknown Portable Text values** (Sanity Studio v6.16.0, Sep 22, 2026) — Portable Text fields containing values the schema doesn't recognize no longer crash the editor, alongside auth, release, and presence fixes. Still the first thing to check on "the editor went blank" reports from customers on older 6.x. → [Changelog entry](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/studio-Ni4xNS4w)

## :mega: Company news

* **What's new in September: trustworthy agents, security improvements, and new integrations** (Sep 22, 2026) — the monthly roundup covers Content Agent for Linear (agents handling editorial tasks inside Linear issues), `sanity.new` for provisioning a project without an account first (with a 72-hour window for a human to claim it), and a new organization-level Security tab surfacing CORS origins, non-expiring API tokens, dataset visibility, admin access, and SAML coverage. → [Read the post](https://www.sanity.io/blog/whats-new-september-releases)
* **Everything we shipped so you can trust agents with your content** (Sep 14, 2026) — the Everything conference recap announcing Knowledge Bases, Workflows in beta, Content Variants, Durable Functions, and the Sanity Labs initiatives. → [Read the post](https://www.sanity.io/blog/everything-we-shipped-so-you-can-trust-agents-with-your-content)

## :bulb: Sanity tip of the day

**Count related documents without fetching them**

When a customer complains a listing query is slow or the response is enormous, check whether they are pulling whole arrays of related documents just to show a number. `count()` runs inside a projection and returns the count without transferring the documents, so the query below gives you the tally per author while returning nothing but names and integers. The `^` refers to the enclosing document, which is what makes the correlated subquery work.

```groq
*[_type == "author"]{
  name,
  "postCount": count(*[_type == "post" && references(^._id)])
}
```

Pair it with `defined()` when the field may be missing — `count(*[_type == "post" && defined(publishedAt) && references(^._id)])` — so unpublished drafts don't inflate the number.

title: Sanity Deep Dive
body:
# Sanity Deep Dive — The webhook that didn't fire, and the one that fired ten thousand times

*Diagnose a silent or runaway GROQ-powered webhook from the filter, the logs, and the delivery headers, without guessing.*

Tuesday, September 29, 2026 · Webhooks · Support engineering

::: {.callout}
**The short version.** A GROQ-powered webhook has two independent failure surfaces: whether the change matched the filter at all, and whether the delivery reached the customer's endpoint. The filter side is dominated by one default — documents in the `drafts.` and `versions.` ID namespaces are ignored unless explicitly enabled — so "I edited it and nothing happened" is usually "you edited a draft." The delivery side is dominated by a limit that changed recently: as of the `v2021-10-04` webhook change on April 29, 2026, Sanity retries a failed delivery **twice at 30-second intervals** and then gives up. That is about a minute of tolerance, not the 30-minute exponential backoff customers may remember.
:::

## Why this comes up

The tickets arrive in two shapes, and they sound nothing alike.

The first is silence. "I changed the document and my site didn't rebuild." "Our Slack notification stopped working last week and we didn't change anything." The customer is certain the webhook is broken, and the webhook is usually fine — it simply never matched.

The second is a flood. "We got 40,000 requests from Sanity in an hour and it took our API down." "The attempts log shows everything queued and nothing is delivering." This one is almost always a filter that is too broad combined with draft triggering switched on, because in Studio nearly every keystroke is an `update` on a draft document.

A third, quieter variant is worth naming because it produces the most confusing thread: the webhook fires, the endpoint returns 200, and the customer still sees stale data. That is a payload or ordering problem, not a delivery problem, and it is diagnosed completely differently.

## How it actually works

A GROQ-powered webhook is not a general event stream with a filter bolted on. It is two GROQ expressions evaluated against a single document mutation, and understanding that the evaluation is *per-document and local* explains most of the surprising behavior.

**The filter** is the part you would normally write between `*[` and `]`. It runs against the document that changed. If you leave it empty it matches everything (`*[]`). Critically, the filter is evaluated without access to the rest of the dataset: sub-queries and cross-dataset references are not supported and yield `false` rather than erroring. A filter like `_type == "book" && author._ref in *[_type == "author" && name == "John Doe"]._id` does not fail loudly — it silently never matches. That silence is exactly what a "my webhook stopped working" ticket looks like from the outside.

**The projection** shapes the request body. It has the same locality constraint: you can follow references out of the triggering document with `->`, as deep as you like, but you cannot reach sideways into unrelated documents. `{ "relatedPost": *[^._id in related[]._ref]{_id, title} }` is the canonical example of a projection that will not work. Leave the projection empty and you get the whole document as it exists *after* the change.

Both fields get Delta-GROQ on top of ordinary GROQ: `before()` and `after()` give you the pre- and post-change document, and `delta::changedAny()` / `delta::changedOnly()` let you trigger only when specific fields moved. One asymmetry trips people up — you can project off `before()` and `after()` (`before(){ name, price }`) but you cannot compare them as objects in a *filter*, because objects are not compared by value there, so `==` is always false and `!=` is always true. Compare individual fields instead.

**The drafts default** is the single highest-yield thing to know. Documents whose IDs live in the `drafts.` or `versions.` namespaces are ignored by default. That is why publishing fires a webhook and editing does not. Turning the setting on ("Trigger webhook when versions are modified" in Manage, or `includeAllVersions: true` via the Webhooks API, requiring webhook API version `v2025-02-19` or later) is what converts a well-behaved webhook into a firehose.

**Delivery** is deliberately conservative. Sanity sends one request at a time per webhook — deliveries are never parallel — with a 30-second timeout. Success is a 200-range response. A 400-range response is treated as undeliverable and is **never retried**; only 429 and 500-range responses are retried, twice, 30 seconds apart. Because one webhook is one serial queue, a slow handler does not cause parallel load; it causes the queue to fall behind and, if changes keep arriving faster than the handler responds, never clear.

Delivery is *at-least-once*, which is why every request carries an `idempotency-key` header. A receiver that does not de-duplicate on it will eventually double-process something.

## Walk it through

Take the runaway case: a customer triggers a rebuild on every product change and is drowning in requests.

The filter they wrote:

```groq
_type == "product"
```

With draft triggering enabled, this matches every autosave of every product. The fix is to narrow on both axes — the fields that actually matter, and the published-only default:

```groq
_type == "product" && delta::changedAny((title, slug, price, stock))
```

Note the double parentheses when listing more than one field; a single set is a common syntax slip. If the rebuild only cares about *content* changes and should ignore a `featured` toggle flipped by an automation, invert it:

```groq
_type == "product" && !delta::changedOnly(featured)
```

Now the payload. The default payload is the whole post-change document, which is wasteful and leaks fields. A projection that gives the receiving system exactly what it needs, including where the request came from:

```groq
{
  _id,
  _type,
  "slug": slug.current,
  "authorName": author->name,
  "priceBefore": before().price,
  "priceAfter": after().price,
  "projectId": sanity::projectId(),
  "dataset": sanity::dataset()
}
```

Then verification on the receiving end. Sanity never transmits the secret. It signs the payload and sends `sanity-webhook-signature` formatted `t=<timestamp>,v1=<signature>`, where the signature is an HMAC-SHA256 of `<timestamp>.<raw request body>`, base64url-encoded — the same scheme Stripe uses. The failure mode here is subtle and extremely common:

```ts
// WRONG — the body has already been parsed and re-serialized,
// so the bytes no longer match what was signed.
app.use(express.json())
app.post('/hook', (req, res) => {
  verify(JSON.stringify(req.body), req.headers['sanity-webhook-signature'])
})

// RIGHT — verify against the raw, unparsed body, then parse.
app.post('/hook', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), (req, res) => {
  verify(req.body, req.headers['sanity-webhook-signature'])
  const payload = JSON.parse(req.body.toString('utf8'))
})
```

Any middleware that parses JSON before verification will produce mismatches on payloads that are perfectly valid. If a customer reports "signature verification fails intermittently," this is the first thing to check — it often looks intermittent because it only breaks on payloads where re-serialization changes key order or whitespace.

The `sanity-io/webhook-toolkit` library handles this correctly and is worth pointing customers at rather than having them roll their own.

## Where it goes wrong

|Symptom|Cause|Fix|
|  ---  |  ---  |  ---  |
|Webhook never fires on edit, fires on publish|`drafts.` and `versions.` documents are ignored by default|Expected behavior. Only enable version triggering if the integration genuinely needs unpublished content — warn about volume|
|Filter silently matches nothing|Sub-query or cross-dataset reference in the filter; these yield `false` rather than erroring|Rewrite using only fields and `->` joins reachable from the triggering document|
|Projection returns null for related content|Sub-queries are unsupported in projections too|Follow a real reference with `->`, or send the `_id` and have the receiver query for the rest|
|Endpoint returns 400, deliveries never retry|400-range is treated as undeliverable by design|If the receiver is overloaded, return 429 or a 5xx so the retry policy applies. Never return 4xx for a transient problem|
|Everything stuck at `queued` in the message log|Handler is slower than the rate of triggering changes, or the filter is too broad|Narrow the filter; acknowledge receipt immediately and process asynchronously via a queue|
|Signature verification fails on valid payloads|Body parsed before verification|Verify against the raw request body|
|Receiver processed the same change twice|Delivery is at-least-once|De-duplicate on the `idempotency-key` header|
|Data in the payload is stale or applied out of order|Deliveries can be delayed and can arrive out of order|Compare `_updatedAt`, or treat the webhook as a signal to re-query rather than as the source of truth|

## Triage checklist

1. Open the **attempts log** (three-dot menu on the webhook in Manage, or `GET https://${projectId}.api.sanity.io/v2021-10-04/hooks/projects/${projectId}/${id}/attempts`). Were there attempts at all? This single question splits the whole problem space.
2. **No attempts** means nothing matched. Confirm whether the customer edited a draft rather than publishing. Then read the filter for sub-queries or cross-dataset references, which fail silently.
3. **Attempts with 400-range responses** means the customer's endpoint rejected it and it was never retried. Get the response body from the log — it is usually an auth header or a content-type problem on their side.
4. **Attempts with 429 or 5xx** means it was retried twice, 30 seconds apart, and then dropped. Ask what their reconciliation path is; with a roughly one-minute tolerance window, they need one.
5. **No attempts but the webhook is clearly firing** — check the **message log** (`GET https://${projectId}.api.sanity.io/v2021-10-04/hooks/${id}/messages`). All `queued` means processing has fallen behind, not that delivery is broken.
6. For payload complaints, compare the projection against what the endpoint received. Remember the projection always serializes as JSON; any other content type needs a function in between.
7. Check the `sanity-transaction-time` header on a recent delivery against when the change was made, to distinguish a delivery delay from a filter miss.
8. **Branch.** If the filter, the drafts setting, the response codes, or the verification order explain the behavior, it is configuration and you can resolve it in-thread. If the attempts log shows successful 200 deliveries that the customer's system demonstrably never received, or messages queued with no attempts over a sustained period and a narrow filter, escalate with the webhook ID, project ID, and a transaction ID from the logs.

::: {.callout}
**For the customer.** Sanity webhooks ignore draft and unpublished-version documents by default, so a webhook will fire when you publish a change but not while you are editing. If you need it to react to unpublished edits, there is a setting for that, but be aware it fires on nearly every keystroke and can generate a very large volume of requests. On delivery: we send one request at a time and wait up to 30 seconds for a response. If your endpoint returns a 429 or a 500-range status we retry twice, 30 seconds apart, and then stop; a 400-range response is treated as a permanent rejection and is not retried at all. Because that retry window is short, we recommend a periodic sync job that catches anything missed — querying on `_updatedAt` since your last sync is the usual approach. Finally, deliveries are at-least-once, so use the `idempotency-key` header we send to avoid processing the same change twice.
:::

## Going deeper

* [GROQ-powered webhooks](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/webhooks) — configuration reference, the full header list, idempotency, and the technical limits.
* [Webhook best practices](https://www.sanity.io/docs/content-lake/webhook-best-practices) — reconciliation, scalability, and the signature verification details.
* [Intro to Projections](https://www.sanity.io/docs/developer-guides/projections-in-groq-powered-webhooks) — shaping payloads, Delta-GROQ, and the `sanity::` namespace.
* [Intro to Filters](https://www.sanity.io/docs/developer-guides/filters-in-groq-powered-webhooks) — `delta::changedAny()`, `delta::changedOnly()`, and the object-comparison caveat.
* [Webhooks API reference](https://www.sanity.io/docs/http-reference/webhooks) — managing webhooks and reading the attempts and message logs programmatically.
* [sanity-io/webhook-toolkit](https://github.com/sanity-io/webhook-toolkit) — signature verification utilities.
* [Webhook egress IP addresses](https://www.sanity.io/files/webhooks-egress-ips.txt) — for customers doing IP allowlisting. These change occasionally; planned changes are announced about seven days ahead on the status page, unplanned ones are not, so the list must be consumed automatically.

Related changelog entries:

* [Webhooks now retry twice at 30-second intervals](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/50ec6abf-fe0c-475b-ae72-314148860132) — April 29, 2026. Replaced the previous 30-minute exponential backoff. This is the one customers have not internalized.
* [Webhooks now support version documents](https://www.sanity.io/docs/changelog/4c78806d-0725-4b01-bf75-307c97548c3f) — April 23, 2025. Added the `versions.` namespace handling, from webhook API version `v2025-02-19`.

Adjacent topic worth knowing: [Sanity Functions](https://www.sanity.io/docs/functions/functions-introduction) run on Sanity's infrastructure and remove the endpoint from the equation entirely. For customers whose webhook problem is fundamentally "we do not want to operate a receiver," that is often the better answer than tuning a filter.
